![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14193250/assets/72e1d1f1ea1aa635441da5503a49ac4d33d5ab0df62d48aa699debc7816df1c2.png)

Which of the following statements are true regarding the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above? 

I. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-2+h)-f(-2)}{h}=1$

II. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}=-0.5$

III. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-3+h)-f(-3)}{h}=1$
questions.worked_solution:
Comparing these limits with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

we see that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-2+h)-f(-2)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(-2), \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(0), \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-3+h)-f(-3)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(-3).\end{aligned}
$$

The function consists of three line segments. Inspecting the graph, we see that

- for $x<-1$, we have  ${f}^{′}(x)=1,$

- for $-1<x<1$, we have  ${f}^{′}(x)=-1,$

- for $x>1$, we have  ${f}^{′}(x)=1.$

The derivative does not exist at $x=-1$ and $x=1$ . So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-2+h)-f(-2)}{h} & =1, \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} & =-1, \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-3+h)-f(-3)}{h} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only I and III are true.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we let

$$
L={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{{x}^{2}-4}{x-2}.
$$

Comparing this with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a},
$$

we see that if we let $f(x)={x}^{2}$ and $a=2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{f(x)-f(2)}{x-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{{x}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{x-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{{x}^{2}-4}{x-2}=L.\end{aligned}
$$

This confirms that $L={f}^{′}(2).$

Computing the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=2x,\,{f}^{′}(2)=2\cdot 2=4,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $L=4.$

Which of the following statements are true regarding the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above?

I. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}=0$

II. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=-1$

III. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h}=-1$
questions.worked_solution:
Comparing these limits with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

we see that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(0), \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(1), \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(3).\end{aligned}
$$

The function consists of three line segments. Inspecting the graph, we see that

- for $-4<x<-1$, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=-1,$

- for $-1<x<1$, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$

- for $1<x<4$, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=-1,$

 The derivative does not exist at $x=\pm 1.$ So, we have  

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} & =0, \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h} & =\text{DNE}, \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we let

$$
L={lim}_{x\to \pi /4}\,\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{x-\frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

Comparing this with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a},
$$

we see that if we let $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)$ and $a=\frac{\pi }{4}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={lim}_{x\to \pi /4}\frac{f(x)-f\,(\frac{\pi }{4})}{x-\frac{\pi }{4}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)-cos\,(\frac{\pi }{4})}{x-\frac{\pi }{4}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{x-\frac{\pi }{4}}=L.\end{aligned}
$$

 

This confirms that $L={f}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{4}).$

Computing the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\,{f}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{4})=-sin\,(\frac{\pi }{4})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},
$$

and therefore, we conclude that $L=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$
